posts.body_html:
Wanted to compare the two darkest plants in the collection, both of which I've posted before: one is Jerry Addington's "Raven" and the other is Mike's "Black" which kicked off this whole thread. Both are grown under identical conditions (full sun outdoors in the CA Bay Area, zone 9b) and I've had them for about two years.

The verdict? Both are absolutely phenomenal clones. For what it's worth, "Raven" is currently slightly darker. As the season progresses, maybe that will change (Mike told me that the darkest colors on "Black" occur when temps cool down in late fall) but for now the colors of the pitchers are holding fairly stable. "Raven" also colors up much faster, with the pitchers opening already a deep red and getting black quickly thereafter. The colors of "Black" are slightly more muted, and the subtle fuzziness of the pitchers gives the whole plant an almost charcoal gray cast. Its shape and stature are magnificent though, and the plant absolutely looms like a shadow in its table. Not crazy tall, but very thick/robust pitcher growth. A huge mature clump of this will be INCREDIBLE. 

Note: For the sake of transparency, these photos have not been edited at all, and I tried to expose them all as accurately as possible. Since most were taken at dusk, they do have a slightly bluish overall cast, which can make the color of the plants looking slightly more jet black than they appear in person (the true undertones are more red and purple). I mainly just wanted to get some good documentation of these while they're in their prime. Enjoy the photos!


"Black" on the left, "Raven" on the right:


Another side-by-side. "Raven" definitely looks darker here. Note the difference in developing pitcher color/vividness:


One more group shot. These deep black pitchers photograph super well, especially at dawn/dusk when the light is soft and diffuse instead of harsh direct sun.


"Raven" by itself. Hard to get much gnarlier than that:


A few shots of "Black" looking majestic AF--that does NOT stand for anthocyanin free, folks...




And finally, both plants compared to purp venosa "minor black" which is luxuriously dark for a purp in July but certainly not deep blackish like these heavy hitters!



I'll keep updating the thread as the season progresses, but for now, let me know what you think! Which clone do you prefer?

posts.body_html:
Not the best shots, but thought I'd compare winter colors between "Black" and "Raven"

The verdict? Raven stays wayyy darker, at least in my conditions. Black still looks beautiful and hangs onto its pitchers very well, but they bleach out to a deep red. Raven, meanwhile, stays nearly as dark as its peak season color, albeit slightly bleached, but the mouth stays so black it almost looks blue.

Raven left, Black right:


A better shot of Raven next to a purp hybrid I made to show what some "normal" plants look like now:

posts.body_html: Here's a quick cell phone shot of Black at dusk. It's extremely dark this year, maybe even a little ahead of Raven as of now. That said, it's hard to compare the two clones directly, as the base color of Black is a little more of a ruddy reddish brown compared to the saturated red of Raven, and Black is also slightly pubescent which can give the pitchers almost a charcoal gray cast in certain lighting. Stunning nonetheless, and I made a huge number of crosses with it this year. Time for the next generation of crazy dark Sarracenia!

posts.body_html:
As for the dark one, it continues to darken even if the cell of the camera has great difficulty in “capturing” these obscure harmonics and declines in violet/crimson/wine lees which is closer to black for the human eye. This is how it is, even technology has its limits. The dark purple veins along the urn end in matte black on the operculum (fairly visible on the peaks). In addition to the waxy covering of the operculum, the plant secretes a lot of shiny nectar which participates in the chromatic modification by reflecting the light.

Fortunately, witnesses, “Live” & in good faith, are able to attest to the dark side of the pitchers. The fact remains that to date, it is the darkest plant in my collection. From next year his genes will be used to further darken, if possible, what can be…
